<reason>Side A (CON) drove the agenda with the European repeal record and converted it into a live burden: asked directly which design feature distinguished this proposal from the failed taxes, Side B answered it could not identify one. Side B's recovery—repeal is political, not an evaluation of this rate/threshold/coverage combination—was honest but only partially blunted A's "this time must differ" framing, and sat in mild tension with the admission itself. Side B's best material (the deferral-accrual distinction showing deferred liabilities differ from a single estate measurement, and the point that listed shares defeat both valuation and mobility objections) was genuinely strong and never fully neutralized, and A conceded its borrowing-alternative has real enforcement seams. But A's rejoinder—that the tax collects hardest where enforcement is weakest and duplicates estate taxation where it works—kept the comparison tilted. A's clipped Rebuttal 2 and its admitted difficulty tracing debt-financed consumption are execution costs, keeping this clear but competitive rather than a solid win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was A's Q2 (which missing design feature would have saved France, Germany, and Sweden?) forcing B's candid "I cannot reliably identify a single missing feature," which A then weaponized in Rebuttal 2 and the Closing as proof the burden of justification was never met; B's strongest counter was the B4.1 distinction that annually accruing deferred obligations differ economically from a one-time estate measurement.</best_rebuttal>
